title: OCD 4 — Test
src: Sterilization & disinfection — principles, methods & clinical application

mcqs.q: Sterilization is best defined as:
opts: Complete destruction of all microorganisms including spores
mcqs.explain: Sterilization destroys ALL microorganisms including spores; disinfection eliminates pathogens EXCEPT spores.

mcqs.q: The key difference between disinfection and sterilization is that disinfection does NOT reliably kill:
mcqs.explain: Disinfection eliminates many/all pathogens except bacterial spores, which only sterilization destroys.

mcqs.q: Which agent is used for HIGH-level disinfection?
mcqs.explain: High-level disinfection (e.g. 2% glutaraldehyde, hydrogen peroxide) destroys bacteria, HIV/HBV and fungi.

mcqs.q: Intermediate-level disinfection kills TB but NOT spores and uses agents such as:
mcqs.explain: Intermediate-level disinfection (70% ethyl/isopropyl alcohol, phenolics) kills the TB bacillus but not spores; used on chair and X-ray surfaces.

mcqs.q: This image shows chemical disinfectant products. Low-level disinfection is appropriate for:
mcqs.explain: Low-level disinfectants (chlorhexidine, dilute phenolics) are for non-critical, non-clinical surfaces like floors and walls.

mcqs.q: In the Spaulding classification, instruments that penetrate soft tissue or bone are:
mcqs.explain: Critical instruments (forceps, elevators, surgical burs, scalpels, endo files) penetrate tissue/bone and must be sterilized.

mcqs.q: A mouth mirror or dental probe that contacts mucous membranes is classed as:
mcqs.explain: Semi-critical items contact mucosa and require high-level disinfection or sterilization (mirrors, handpieces, probes, trays).

mcqs.q: This image shows dental instruments. A blood-pressure cuff or light handle is classed as:
mcqs.explain: Non-critical items contact only intact skin (BP cuff, chair surfaces, light handle, X-ray panel) and need disinfection.

mcqs.q: Dry-heat sterilization in a hot-air oven requires which time at 160°C?
At 180°C, the dry-heat holding time is:
mcqs.explain: Higher temperature needs less time: 180°C → 30 minutes.

mcqs.q: This image shows a hot-air oven. Dry heat is NOT suitable for:
mcqs.explain: Dry heat suits glassware, metals, sharps, powders and oils, but NOT heat-sensitive rubber, plastic or fabric.

mcqs.q: The autoclave sterilizes using:
mcqs.explain: The autoclave uses steam + pressure + heat at 121–134°C; moist heat denatures microbial proteins.

mcqs.q: A major advantage of the autoclave over dry heat and most disinfectants is that it:
mcqs.explain: Moist heat under pressure kills bacteria, viruses, fungi AND spores — the autoclave is the dental gold standard.

mcqs.q: This image shows an autoclave. A disadvantage of steam sterilization is that it may:
mcqs.explain: Steam can cause rusting/corrosion of carbon-steel instruments, though it reliably sterilizes including spores.

mcqs.q: Chemical vapor sterilization (chemiclave) operates at about:
mcqs.explain: The chemiclave uses chemical vapors (alcohol, formaldehyde, ketone) plus heat at ~132°C.

mcqs.q: This image shows a chemiclave. Its main ADVANTAGE over the autoclave is:
mcqs.explain: Chemical vapor causes less rusting/corrosion, making it good for metal instruments; its drawback is toxic vapors needing ventilation.

mcqs.q: A disadvantage of the chemiclave is that it:
opts: Produces toxic vapors and needs good ventilation
mcqs.explain: The toxic chemical vapors require good ventilation, which is why the chemiclave is less commonly used today.

mcqs.q: Ultraviolet light and periodic formaldehyde/hydrogen-peroxide fogging are used for:
mcqs.explain: Air/environment control uses UV light after hours, ventilation and periodic fumigation (fogging) weekly/monthly.

mcqs.q: Dental unit waterlines (DUWL) should be flushed daily mainly to:
mcqs.explain: Daily flushing plus chemical waterline disinfectants prevents biofilm formation in the DUWL.

mcqs.q: Typical room turnover time for a routine dental procedure is about:
mcqs.explain: Routine procedures need ~10–15 min turnover; surgical/aerosol-generating procedures need ~15–30 min.

mcqs.q: The Hepatitis B vaccination schedule for dental staff is:
opts: 0, 1 and 6 months with a booster every 5 years
mcqs.explain: HBV: 0, 1, 6 months, booster every 5 years; anti-HBs is checked and the course repeated if antibody is low/absent.

mcqs.q: After HBV vaccination, protection is confirmed by testing for:
mcqs.explain: Anti-HBs antibody level confirms immunity; if low/absent, vaccination is repeated.

mcqs.q: This image shows a healthcare worker being vaccinated. For which infection is there NO vaccine for dental staff?
mcqs.explain: There is no vaccine for HCV or HIV; HBV, influenza, MMR and varicella vaccines are available.

mcqs.q: The varicella-zoster vaccine for those over 13 years is given as:
mcqs.explain: Varicella vaccine = two doses 4–8 weeks apart for those older than 13 years.

mcqs.q: First aid for a PERCUTANEOUS sharps injury is:
opts: Wash with soap and water, apply 70% isopropyl alcohol, then bandage
Apply pressure only and continue working
mcqs.explain: Percutaneous injury: wash with water and soap → 70% isopropyl alcohol → bandage; then report.

mcqs.q: For a mucocutaneous (eye splash) exposure, you should:
opts: Irrigate the eye with clean water/saline and flush for 10 minutes
Do nothing if it doesn't hurt
mcqs.explain: Flush splashes and irrigate the eye with clean sterile water or saline, flushing the site for about 10 minutes.

mcqs.q: Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for a blood exposure is primarily determined by the:
mcqs.explain: After reporting and consulting a physician, PEP is determined largely by the source's HBsAg status.

mcqs.q: In dental radiology, semicritical film holders and PID should be:
mcqs.explain: Film holders/PID are semicritical: disposable, heat-sterilized or high-level disinfected between patients.

mcqs.q: This image shows protecting the film packet. Before removing gloves after exposing a film you should:
opts: Dry the film with gauze to remove blood/saliva
mcqs.explain: Dry the film with gauze to remove blood/saliva before degloving; if pouches are used, remove the film without contaminating it.

mcqs.q: Which sequence correctly ranks the processes from most to least lethal to microbes?
mcqs.explain: Sterilization (kills spores) > high-level disinfection > intermediate > low-level disinfection > simple cleaning.

saqs.q: Define sterilization and disinfection and state the key difference.
saqs.a: Sterilization = complete destruction of all microorganisms including spores. Disinfection = elimination of pathogens except spores. Key difference: only sterilization reliably kills spores.

saqs.q: Give the Spaulding classification of dental instruments with the required process for each.
Compare dry heat, autoclave and chemiclave (temperature and one key feature each).
saqs.a:
MethodTempKey
Dry heat160–180°Cno moisture; not for rubber/plastic
Autoclave121–134°Ckills spores; may rust steel
Chemiclave~132°Clow corrosion; toxic vapors

saqs.q: List the three levels of disinfection with an example agent and use for each.
saqs.a: High — 2% glutaraldehyde/H₂O₂ (kills HIV/HBV, fungi). Intermediate — 70% alcohol/phenolics (TB, chair & X-ray surfaces). Low — chlorhexidine/dilute phenolics (floors, walls).

saqs.q: Outline the immunizations recommended for dental healthcare personnel.
saqs.a: Hepatitis B (0,1,6 months + booster q5y, check anti-HBs), influenza (annual), MMR, varicella (2 doses). There is no vaccine for HCV or HIV.

saqs.q: A clinician sustains a needlestick injury from a used needle. Outline the immediate first-aid and reporting steps.
saqs.a: Wash the site with soap and water, apply 70% isopropyl alcohol, bandage. Report and record the injury, consult a physician immediately; PEP is determined by the source's HBsAg status.
